title: On the Tightness and Computational Tractability of Higher-Dimensional Confidence Sequences
claim: A cheap-to-compute outer approximation tightly encloses the intractable confidence region and is far smaller than the data spread or baseline.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, dashed zoom lines linking overview to detail
description: Two panels. Panel (a), "Overview", is a 2-D scatter on [0,1] axes. Gray × marks show observations spread horizontally around y≈0.5. A large blue-purple circle, the baseline region, surrounds a tiny rectangle near (0.4, 0.5). Black dashed lines run from this rectangle to the large dashed frame of panel (b), "Confidence region detail". Panel (b) shows the zoomed region. A light-blue dotted fill, the intractable portfolio region, is enclosed by an orange bounding box, a blue ellipse and a magenta rounded-rectangle intersection. A filled black dot (empirical mean) and an open circle (population mean) sit inside it. The eye goes first to the zoom lines and the large detail panel, then to the contrast between the huge baseline circle and the tiny region.

abstract: Modern sequential monitoring problems often involve multiple metrics, where we monitor several data streams simultaneously and may act once the evidence is strong enough. Confidence sequences (CSs) are a natural tool for such continuous monitoring. However, for bounded vector means, existing multivariate CSs are either tight but computationally intractable, or fast to compute but conservative. To address this, we study three lifts of one-dimensional betting-based CSs to higher dimensions: a weighted Bonferroni region, an equivalent max-wealth form, and a portfolio region. The portfolio is typically much tighter, especially in higher dimensions, but its boundary and properties such as volume are not available in closed form. To make this tighter construction usable, we propose tractable outer approximations of the portfolio region that preserve statistical validity: a bounding box, an $\ell_p$-ellipsoid, and their intersection. We prove set relations among all constructions and show empirically that these approximations (i) achieve regions close to the intractable portfolio, (ii) substantially outperform existing tractable multivariate CSs, and (iii) enable practical use cases such as multi-metric A/B testing and model comparison.
